lead: Sequential data is a list where position matters: x₁, x₂, …, x_T. A sequence learning problem takes such a list and returns one label, a label for every step, or a new list. The length T can change from one example to the next. Text, speech, sensor logs and video all arrive in this form. This chapter fixes the vocabulary, separates the three output shapes, and shows how to cut a series into supervised examples without cheating by looking into the future.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 for supervised learning and labels; Unit 3 for CNN features if video is mentioned. The recurrent model that consumes order is in 4.2.

blocks.text: A sequence is data where the index carries meaning. We write x<sub>t</sub> for the value at time step t. The length is T, so the sequence is x₁, x₂, …, x<sub>T</sub>. A sensor may record x₁ = 2, x₂ = 4, x₃ = 6 at three time steps.
Length is often variable. One sentence has T = 8 words, another has T = 21 words. A speech clip has T frames, and a sensor log has T samples. T can differ for every example in the dataset.

Order matters. If you shuffle the sensor values [2, 4, 6, 8, 10], the rising trend disappears. In text, “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” contain the same words in a different order and mean different things. A model that ignores t treats both sentences as one bag of words.

A sequence learning problem learns a function from x₁ … x<sub>T</sub> to an output. The output can be one label y, a label for every step y₁ … y<sub>T</sub>, or a new sequence y₁ … y<sub>U</sub>. The output length U may equal T or may differ.

Video adds two dimensions, space and time. CNN features plus a recurrent layer is one way to model video, but spatio-temporal action recognition is advanced; only a few universities teach it in detail, so it stays a one-line note here and in 4.7.

items: Many-to-one classification. The whole sequence gives one label. A review gives sentiment positive or negative. A sensor log gives fault or no-fault. The model reads all T steps and produces a fixed-size output, often from the last hidden state in 4.2.

Many-to-many labelling, same length. Every input step gets a tag. Part-of-speech tagging labels each word as noun, verb, adjective and so on. Named-entity recognition labels each word as person, place, organisation or other. Input length T equals output length T, and step t aligns with tag yt.

Many-to-many sequence-to-sequence. The input is one sequence and the output is another sequence, often with U ≠ T. Translation reads an English sentence of length T and writes a Tamil sentence of length U. Speech-to-text reads audio frames and writes words. The encoder-decoder model in 4.5 handles this shape.

blocks.text: The same data can be framed in more than one way. A product review can be classified as positive or negative, or every word can be tagged as complaint or praise. Choose the shape by what you must predict and what information is available at prediction time. For translation, no target words are known before generation starts. For tagging, every input word is visible.

For forecasting, turn one series into supervised pairs with a sliding window. Pick a window length w. The input is [x<sub>t</sub>, x<sub>t+1</sub>, …, x<sub>t+w−1</sub>] and the target is the next value x<sub>t+w</sub>. Slide the window one step to the right and repeat. The figure shows w = 3 on five values.

blocks.where: N is the number of values in the series; w is the window length; N<sub>pairs</sub> is the number of (input window, next value) pairs.

blocks.text: Models train on rectangular batches, so short sequences are padded to the maximum length in the batch. Padding adds dummy steps, often zeros or a special pad token. A mask marks real steps and padded steps. The loss ignores padded steps; without a mask the model learns to predict padding.

Split sequential data by time, not by random rows. Train on earlier time, validate and test on later time. Keep every window inside one split. A window that crosses the split boundary carries future values into training. Do not shuffle time steps before splitting; that leaks future information into the training set.

figure.caption: A window of 3 values predicts the next one: [2, 4, 6] → 8, then one step later [4, 6, 8] → 10. Five values give only 5 − 3 = 2 pairs.

spec.aria: The series 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 in five cells, with two overlapping windows of three values below it, each pointing at its target 8 and 10.

examples.question: A sensor records x = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] at t = 1 … 5. Use windows of length 3 to predict the next value. List every (input window, target) pair and give the number of pairs.
steps: The series has N = 5 values and the window length is w = 3.
First window starts at t = 1: input [x₁, x₂, x₃] = [2, 4, 6]. The next value is x₄ = 8. Pair: ([2, 4, 6] → 8).
Slide one step. Second window starts at t = 2: input [x₂, x₃, x₄] = [4, 6, 8]. The next value is x₅ = 10. Pair: ([4, 6, 8] → 10).
A third window would start at t = 3 and need x₆, which does not exist. Stop.
examples.answer: The two training pairs are ([2, 4, 6] → 8) and ([4, 6, 8] → 10), so there are 2 pairs.

traps: Shuffling time steps or splitting a time series by random rows leaks future values into training. Split by time and keep windows inside each split.
Padding without a mask changes the loss: the model is rewarded for predicting pad tokens. Mask padded steps so only real steps count.
Many-to-one classification returns one label for the whole sequence. Seq2seq returns a new sequence and can have a different output length U. Do not use the names as synonyms.
For a next-value task with N values and window length w, the number of pairs is N − w. Counting N − w + 1 includes a window that has no target.
Variable length is normal. Padding makes a batch rectangular but does not change the true length T of each example.

quiz.q: Define time step t and sequence length T.
quiz.a: Time step t is the position of one value in the sequence. Sequence length T is the total number of steps, so the sequence is x₁ … x<sub>T</sub>.

quiz.q: Why does shuffling time steps damage a sequence model?
quiz.a: Shuffling destroys the order that carries meaning. Neighbouring values no longer follow each other, trends and context disappear, and the model cannot learn from previous steps.

quiz.q: Series x = [3, 6, 9, 12, 15]. Window length 2 predicts the next value. List all (window, target) pairs.
A sensor log has N = 100 values and window length w = 10 for next-value prediction. How many training pairs?
A team splits a time series by random rows into 80% train and 20% test, then builds windows. State the leakage and give a correct split.
quiz.a: Random rows put later values into training and earlier values into test, so the model sees the future. Correct split: sort by time, train on the earlier segment, test on the later segment, and keep windows from crossing the boundary.

quiz.q: Task: label each word in a Tamil sentence as noun, verb or other. Which output shape is this? Explain.
quiz.a: This is many-to-many labelling with the same length. Each input word gets one tag at the same step, so T input words produce T output tags. It is not seq2seq because the output is not a new sequence of different length.

quiz.q: Give one reason padding needs a mask.
quiz.a: Padding adds dummy steps so a batch is rectangular. Without a mask, the loss includes those dummy steps and the model learns from pad tokens instead of real data.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, sequence models power demand forecasting, log anomaly detection and speech interfaces. Research moves toward state-space models and temporal convolutional networks that handle very long series. Streaming settings need online updates and drift detection, not one fixed train/test split. Search for “sequence modelling”, “time-series cross-validation” and “state space models” to go further.
